name: Legends Across Every Civilisation
description: Fifty mythical creatures and beings — dragons, giants, sea monsters, tricksters, underworld guides, sky gods, flood survivors, fire-bringers, shape-shifters and the rest — each toured across twenty of the cultures that told a version of it, with twenty materially distinct chapter slots per subject, for long calm compilations that walk one idea around the world.

exclusions: No hooks, cliffhangers, countdowns, teasers, questions to the listener, or promises about what is coming later, at the opening of a chapter or anywhere inside it.
No invented quotations, invented ceremonies, invented tellers, or reconstructed dialogue; describe only what the record supports and say plainly where the record stops.
No claim to restricted or initiated knowledge, and no retelling of material a tradition's own custodians restrict; where such material exists, say that it is held closely and go no further.
No verdict on whether a belief is true or false, no debunking, no ranking of one people's version above another's, and no treatment of a living religion as a dead curiosity.
No dwelling on sacrifice, mutilation, torture, or a violent death; state briefly that it belongs to the account, and give the ceremony, the object, or the aftermath the time instead.
No modern political analogy, no claim about a present-day state, people, religion, or party, and no partisan framing of a contested national tradition.
No living people are named, and no present-day community is described as though its practices were fixed in the past.
Keep every chapter self-contained, resolving to a quiet close, with no reference forward to a later chapter and no callback to an earlier one.
No moralising, no lesson stated at the end, and no direct address urging the listener to think or do anything.
prompt_context: Each chapter tours one mythical being through the version a single culture told of it, and the compilation as a whole walks the same being around the world. Open inside the version rather than at the idea: name the place, name the people who told it, and describe what their creature actually did before saying anything about what creatures mean. Then let the comparison do its own work — a listener who hears a dozen dragons in one night will notice the pattern without being told there is one, and the episode should never announce it. This is a sleep compilation, so keep the tempo even and low: no hook, no question, no promise, no countdown, no cliffhanger, and no sentence at the end of a chapter that points at the next. Favour the concrete and the material over the symbolic — the shape of a carving, the offering left at a well, the wording of a prohibition, the season a ceremony falls in, the object a story leaves behind — and let the interest come from detail rather than from suspense. Say plainly where a tradition is still practised and where it is known only from a record, and treat a living tradition as something people do rather than as a story that has finished. Invent nothing: no quotations from tellers, no imagined ceremonies, no reconstructed dialogue, and no confident claim about what an ancient people believed where the record only shows what they made or wrote. Where the sources disagree, say so quietly and move on; disagreement is interesting, argument is not. Keep every chapter self-contained, so a listener who drifts off at any point has lost nothing and a listener who wakes in the middle can join without being confused. End each chapter on something still — a carved stone, a swept threshold, a cold hearth, a lake at first light — and never on a summary of what it all meant.

evidence_expectations: Ground each chapter in the kind of record named by the slot, and describe record types rather than citing any specific title, author, archive reference, or catalogue number.
Say which of the two the chapter is standing on — something that survives as an object, or something that survives only as a telling — and do not let one borrow the authority of the other.
Where a version is known from a single late source, say so plainly and keep the claims inside what that source can carry.
Where a tradition is still practised, describe the practice in the present and do not convert it into a past-tense curiosity.
Never state a date, a duration, a distance, or a number of any kind more precisely than the record allows.
compatibility_rules: Pair only with the sleep history compilation formula; this pack assumes long, independent chapters with no narrative running between them and no tension carried forward.
Use one subject per episode and never mix two, so that a compilation is one being seen many ways rather than an assortment.
Draw the twenty slots of a subject in any order, but never reuse a slot within one episode set, since each slot is one culture's version and a repeat would be the same chapter twice.
Do not pair with any formula that opens on a hook, builds tension, or ends a chapter pointing forward; the pack's material will not carry it and the exclusions forbid it.
